messages.author: 1d9742508e8aa225
messages.subject: upsidown vectors
parts:
Hi everyone,

I'm struggling with two species of my dataset which seems to have some upside down vector . When I predict the shapes (shape.predictor) for the smallest and largest specimen from the regression scores, I get a perfect adult shape for minimum values, and a neonate shape for maximum values. It's weird that it just happens with two species, and the codes are almost identical for all.

I did something like this for the six species I have analyzed (below).

Could someone tell me why it is happening?

Thanks in advance.

All the best,

Gui


Code (starting from a GPA alignment):


coords.species <- coords.subset(coords.gpa$coords, group = species)

#Lagenorhynchus
coords.gpa.Lalb <- gpagen(coords.species$Lagenorhynchus_albirostris)

fit.Lag <- procD.lm(coords.gpa.Lalb$coords ~ log(coords.gpa.Lalb$Csize), data=coords.gpa.Lalb, iter=0, print.progress = FALSE)

M.Lalb <- mshape(coords.gpa.Lalb$coords)

allom.plot.Lalb <- plot(fit.Lag,
                   type = "regression",
                   predictor = log(coords.gpa.Lalb$Csize),
                   reg.type ="RegScore") 
preds.Lalb <- shape.predictor(fit.Lag$GM$fitted, x= allom.plot.Lalb$RegScore, Intercept =FALSE, predmin = min(allom.plot.Lalb$RegScore), predmax = max(allom.plot.Lalb$RegScore)) 

plotRefToTarget(M.Lalb, preds.Lalb$predmin, mag=3, links = links, method = "points")
plotRefToTarget(M.Lalb, preds.Lalb$predmax, mag=3, links = links, method = "points")

--

messages.author: aab55242ff4da6c6
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] upsidown vectors
parts:
This is just a guess without more evidence but min or max of regression scores does not have to correspond directly to min and max size.  It is possible to have negative scores correspond to large individuals and positive scores correspond to small individuals.  The scores in ordinations are projections on centered vectors, but the vector is arbitrarily orientated with regard to what is negative and positive (i.e., spin the vector 180 degrees and it is the same, but scores would flip from negative to positive and vice versa).

If this makes you uncomfortable you can multiply the scores by -1 before using shape predictor.

Mike

messages.author: 511e44c7d1e1bab0
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] upsidown vectors
parts:
Gui,

this is not a matter of your idea being wrong. If I may give an equivalence to what Mike said, think about PCA vectors: they have no directionality, their polarity is random. In the same way, whether the regression scores are negatively or positively correlated with CS is aleatory. They ARE expressing changes in shape with respect to changes in size (at least, they are one way of doing so) but they are not bound to express changes with INCREASING size. So, to answer your question, you can use this approach to visualize shape changes throughout growth, but MATHEMATICALLY you need to make sure you are fixing the polarity of these changes from small to large organisms. To complicate things further, because you are running analyses for each species separately, the regression score vectors you are calculating are not bound to behave the same way across species, the same way the polarity of PC axes would not necessarily be the same (even if their composition were, but that´s a different issue).

Does this make sense?

Antigoni

messages.author: 511e44c7d1e1bab0
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] upsidown vectors
parts:
And as a complement to my own message, on better thought, if you are interesting in visualizing the FULL set of shape changes related to size variation (allometry), you might be better off using shape.predictor on the allometry lm itself, instead of the reduced-dimension plot of regression scores. Regression scores are useful for visualizing how shape (multivariate) changes with size, mainly in the context of comparing across groups. But if your interest is on the deformations related to growth, I think looking at the full shape space related to size is a better approach.

Antigoni

Hi everyone,

I'm struggling with two species of my dataset which seems to have some upside down vector . When I predict the shapes (shape.predictor) for the smallest and largest specimen from the regression scores, I get a perfect adult shape for minimum values, and a neonate shape for maximum values. I did something like this for the six species I have analyzed (below).

Could someone tell me why it is happening?

Gui


Code (starting from a GPA alignment):


coords.species <- coords.subset(coords.gpa$coords, group = species)

#Lagenorhynchus
coords.gpa.Lalb <- gpagen(coords.species$Lagenorhynchus_albirostris)

fit.Lag <- procD.lm(coords.gpa.Lalb$coords ~ log(coords.gpa.Lalb$Csize), data=coords.gpa.Lalb, iter=0, print.progress = FALSE)

M.Lalb <- mshape(coords.gpa.Lalb$coords)

allom.plot.Lalb <- plot(fit.Lag,
                   type = "regression",
                   predictor = log(coords.gpa.Lalb$Csize),
                   reg.type ="RegScore") 
preds.Lalb <- shape.predictor(fit.Lag$GM$fitted, x= allom.plot.Lalb$RegScore, Intercept =FALSE, predmin = min(allom.plot.Lalb$RegScore), predmax = max(allom.plot.Lalb$RegScore)) 

plotRefToTarget(M.Lalb, preds.Lalb$predmin, mag=3, links = links, method = "points")
plotRefToTarget(M.Lalb, preds.Lalb$predmax, mag=3, links = links, method = "points")
